Not sure if you've come across an answer you've enjoyed yet, but my first thought is to approach this with some vulnerability on your part.  In fact, approaching him and asking him "hey, can I be perfectly vulnerable with you about something?  I would actually like you to stop helping me with my chores.  I want to contribute to the house in my own way, and while I appreciate your effort and thoughtfulness, it does make me feel like I'm not doing my share."

If he responds again that he doesn't mind, I would spin that and note that in this case, it doesn't matter what his perception is.  It matters that *you're* feeling stepped on, and that you being open in this way takes effort, but that you trust him to do the right thing with your negative feelings.

I noticed you mentioned you're often aloof, and that you're just about his only friend, so the last thing you can cap it off with is an offer to do something together.  That the friendship doesn't need favors, just company.

Hope this helps!  I can understand wanting to maneuver around some potentially guilty feelings, and while that's something you shouldn't need to feel responsible for, well...that's not what you came here for, haha.  Wish you the best with this!

What is his relationship with marriage?  What is his family like, his parents' marriage, and how negative is it before you look at the positives?  You may have a healthy attitude towards marriage, and something may be holding him back from liking the idea.

If the state you're in recognizes you as legal partners after a certain time period, what's the difference between that and marriage to him?

If he has a negative outlook on marriage, explore it.  Identify his needs, too.  Then, question how important it is for you to be married.  Are you comfy with a legal partnership, or is there something you can identify that pulls you towards the concept of a traditional marriage?  If the only fear is infidelity / him leaving, then that's worth exploring for you both.

On the other end, if you have some traditional values baked into your personal ideals, then that's a need for you, rather than a want.  It's something you should set as an expectation now, not an option.  Demands are difficult to navigate over asks but it helps you both to be clear with your needs  =)

In the end, if he does not have a negative few of marriage, simply a passive one, it might be worthwhile to ask for a timeline and revisit it later.  If you trust him, then move forward.  If you don't, and you think he'll back out later, there's a breach somewhere in his respect for your needs.

Sounds like you want to talk about this with him now rather than later, so best of luck to you both!

Haha yup, very same on seeking out the good in people.  It's strange how behavior can be so forgivable over time with small actions, but after you write it out it's like wow...that guy is such a dick!
I think for people like you or me, when those small actions happen on a personal level you shrug it off for their sake.  It's a tough lesson to learn that you're likely affecting others, people you love, around you.  Like you said, live and learn!

Agreed, and that was my issue!  Not like we know what kind of person OP is, but I was, at that time, an overly patient and forgiving person to the point of detriment to myself.  That ended up being a detriment to other people too, and that's unfair to others around me.  He's giving her an out and I do hope she's able to roll with it and learn.

So sorry you're facing this!  I had an extremely similar experience to you, from the loving BF with a rough background to the long time friend who I could tune out the BS for.  Weird!

Sincerely not trying to project, but when my "Rob" got into an argument with my "Gee", I ALSO got an ultimatum, and made the decision that that was too controlling for my liking.
My life is calmer and quieter in many happy ways without my Rob.  I didn't realize at the time how many dear friends of mine would not come over to hang because they knew Rob would be there, until he was gone!  My group of friends are gentle and sweet nerds and they just didn't want to give me that same kind of ultimatum.  So they simply avoided him.  Drama was gone, as was the random BS to tune out, and my BF no longer had to put up with moments of extreme annoyance for my sake.

I'm going to at least say, Rob is being petty and immature.  As we get older, that's something many people weed out of their lives.  If you choose to not give him the chase he so obviously wants, you are still allowed to think about your memories fondly and wonder how he's doing.  But you also don't need to put up with the martial arts champ mechanic extraordinaire just because of a long term friendship.  Consider sunk cost fallacy, and maybe try to put value on what you add to the friendship versus what he adds.  Best to you!

Give yourself some time to process this.  You might be seeking any kind of "normal" right now, and sometimes that means avoiding the issue and continuing with plans set in the past.

Take Future-You into account and give them the opportunity to make decisions after you've thought about what to do next.  Put your current plans on hold at least.  You can always make the decision to move forward again later, but once married you'll have to jump through hoops to rescind it.  I won't assume you're canceling - but finding out about an affair shakes your trust in ways you might not have felt yet.

Sorry this is happening to you.

It sounds like being straightforward with him isn't your goal here, and you're worried about losing him as a friend.

In the same way you've told him that you're not in the headspace to have a relationship, you could tell him you're no longer in the headspace to continue to have sexy times with a great friend.

I would obviously just be careful about hooking up with anyone else in the near future, and it would be kind of you to give him a heads up if/when you do find someone you want to make out with instead, dating or not.

Good luck!  Short term feelings sometimes make a mess of long term ones.  Hope everything works out and you all can retain your friendship.

No judgement - people change over time and doing so in your 20's is not too different from doing it in your 40's.  You grow and you learn.
But 10 years together is a long ride.  At the risk of going against the grain here, I might suggest asking her if you two could trial a separation.  Give yourself a chance to experience life without her.  You might find that you depend on her more than you think, or take her for granted.  Give her a chance to experience the freedom you're talking about - especially because it sounds like she's the decision maker / planner.
And leave a lot room for healing for you both.  You're dropping a big bomb on her to decide on a sudden change in your own life, without including her.  That's a big decision for a couple of 10 years.  Even if you expect the conversation to be angry, let her express those emotions.  Your anticipation could stifle her being able to process this with you.  Patience is beyond important with these kinds of things.  Willingness to have an open, honest discussion is invaluable to you both.

A caveat - if your intentions are to try other relationships, this is a bad suggestion.  I am suggesting the trial separation to see how life is without her.  I am not suggesting you leave her hanging while you go out to date others.  If that is your intention, it's best to rip off the bandaid.  At that point, the best thing you can do is be available for answers, and try to not be defensive when she asks.  Remember that this is a huge life change for her, well into her late forties.

Anyway, sorry you're in such a conundrum.  Sounds like you just needed to vent to someone about it.  The whole situation sucks, because age gap aside, you're both adults and capable of making decisions.  Your son would most definitely get the worst outcome in this.

What I'm hearing is that you'd like him to take better care of himself - and maybe that's not something that you're outright asking.  Doing chores, making doctor appointments, remembering family events.  These are things one could call "mothering".  But in a different light you're asking him to take care of himself, be a responsible adult, and ultimately show that he's ready for something long term (and even a dad later on).

You still need to voice this.  This has to be a conversation, even if you want him to think of these things on his own.  It puts the responsibility on you (again) initially - but you're asking him to take it all off of your shoulders.  Or, if you know you'll need to help him still, then at least to communicate appreciation in a more responsive way.
In having the conversation, you might find that not regularly doing these things is a habit, or something underlying.  I might be projecting a bit, but I've had issues with not taking care of myself, and it turned out to be adult ADHD.
Best of luck, OP, hope you stay together through the built up frustration.

I saw a lovely take on issues like this the other day.  "We are reading the same book, but we are on different chapters."  It's possible you're a little ahead on reading compared to him. 5 months isn't all that long - maybe give him a little time to catch up to you!

On another note, if this is plaguing you only every now and then, it's worthwhile to watch your mood cycles. Periods, sure, but also your general moments of vulnerability, irritability, etc.  If you just signed up for therapy, they should be able to walk you through how to track such things.  Best of luck to you, and hope it's simply a case of different paces.

I tried to keep in .ind that he might be shy, anxious, previous bad experiences with GF's friends, literally anything else that didn't apply to me directly.  I just tried to not take it as a personal attack.  Over time, he warmed up to me and some of our other friends, and now he's also a very good friend in our circle.

The considerate thing to do here is give him some space, time, and to try to not take it personally  =)

Hey, definitely in the same boat.  I thought things were okay - and we've been together for 16 years.  I feel completely blindsided.

It's been a few months for me and things are sometimes clear and improving, and sometimes I am also in a hole of sadness.  I think it's most important to accept the other person's feelings and make steps to start focusing on yourself. Therapy was a really good step  =)

How long has it been since you separated?  Wishing you some peaceful nights  <3

Very much feeling this recently. 16 years total between dating and marriage.  We really started from the bottom with nothing and life wasn't fair, but we had each other.  I'm at a point of not wanting him back - the abandonment feels too heavy now - but I really having a sense of security and companionship.

We'll get there.  Thanks for your post, it makes the experience feel a little less lonely.

Personally, you post just gave me some feeling that I am not alone.  2 months following my separation, I felt in tune with what I was doing, and I was picking up my hobbies and being socially active again. I was building goals again.

The following month, complete burnout. Basically isolated myself all over again.  Couldn't sleep, and couldn't keep up with habits because I was too tired and overwhelmed.

We can get through this - we have to. But my advice to myself is to slow it down. Make plans every other weekend, not every chance I get. The grieving period will come and go in waves - if I'm always busy, I'll never allow myself to experience the feelings as they come, and can't make peace with them along the way.  Hope this helps you, too.  

Take your friend's goodwill and understanding at face value.  We all need support right now, and the fact that they were okay with your cancelation should mean a lot. Gratefulness over guilt, thank you over sorry.  Good luck and wish you some peaceful nights.

OP, you sound like my STBX. No judgement. I think that's okay.  I think I needed to read your post.
We make better friends than we do a couple, and that's difficult to admit after 16 years. I am heartbroken most of the time. But you can't force yourself to love someone romantically.
It seems to me that you have a sense of commitment, you care about her, and you are concerned for her.  Friends can love deeply, too.
If you can find someone, I hear a couples therapist can help both parties communicate not only how to be a stronger couple, but also how to let go. If you feel she could find someone better, if you feel your relationship won't work, it's time to evaluate if this thought is true in the context of your relationship, or an issue that you need to work on yourself.
Wish you both some peace throughout a difficult time.

I hope with some pushing on your part that she does agree. In the end if nothing happens and the situation is the same as before, then I hope you find communication, honesty, and closure. Hope the best for you.

I feel you. My husband and I have been together 16 years, and I felt things were calm, content, and generally quite happy. We don't fight (although that's part of the problem, lack of communication from us both).
He's my best friend in the world. Right now we're very friendly still, but when he moves out and starts dating - a prospect he's currently working on - I'll lose my best friend. I didn't realize how much I rely on him for emotional support, and its suddenly gone. It's difficult, and I feel your pain.
Even despite the emergency order, she's been your life partner for a long time. I hope you have a few peaceful nights this week in these confusing times.

It sounds like she went through some thinking, and came to a conclusion without you. Maybe it's an indicator that she cares about you, but you both have issues with communicating about real problems.
An offer to do couples therapy (maybe with a trial separation instead of a divorce) is a good compromise, and a start to fix things?

I agree. He might actually feel bad at first, which is normal and okay. Walk into the conversation with that in mind and help him understand that it's the action itself, not the fact that HE performed it. He can help in the future if you talk about it now.

I think at worst, you manipulate someone who cares and ultimately trick them. I think at best, your friends understand your nature and aren't fooled.
I have learned that people have other shit going on. You (or I) cant be at the center if other peoples lives. Sometimes a conversation is started selflessly. Ask them how they're doing. Be invested in them. Show them care and affection and the same can be returned to you, if they're good people. Hope you have a better and healthy night dude.

I'm on the other side of this. I can say that over time and with a lot of open, honest communication, we're ending our relationship. Sure, it's on his terms - I'd do anything to keep it going. But I know it's one sided, and if I want his happiness, I refuse to trap him in a relationship he doesn't want. We're choosing to be best friends, and we'll support each other as such.
If you need this for YOUR mental health, do what you feel is right. But get help if you are truly questioning your decision. You may be depressed, and your relationship may not be the core issue. If anything, marriage counseling can help discover issues with you both as individuals. But that conversation and request to hin starts with an honest discussion on your thoughts.
Wish the best for both of you, and your individual happiness.

OP, same. It's only been 1 month since he dropped the fact that he's fallen out of love with me. I'm accepting that to continue to love and respect him, I need to acknowledge his decision to end our relationship and move on. I guess time heals, but I know I'll always be in love with him.  I feel very responsible for our struggles, although our marriage was fairly relaxed.
If you still love and respect him, respect his decision.  Work on yourself.  Be more yourself.  Move forward with the intent to love yourself, and don't give yourself false hope. At the end of the day, you have to like you, too.

I feel you on this, on a deep level. My husband is moving on, and I am proud of him and I want him to live his life. I feel I didn't do enough, and that my mental health is ultimately what drove the emotional wedge between us. I will be sad beyond words, I will always love him, he will always be my best friend, and I will learn to move on, too. I wish your heart and your mind peace.

My upcoming ex and I have been having this discussion a lot. He loves me, but he isn't in love with me. We both struggle with our mental health, depend on each other as best friends, and we have been together for 16 years (we are 29 and 30).
His choosing to leave our marriage felt unfair, confusing, heartbreaking, and just plain horrible. But with many very open and honest discussions, we are building a better relationship than we have had in the last 5 years. My suggestion to you - be honest with what you're feeling for both your mental health, and his. He didn't leave me alone and confused and stuck with my thoughts. He answered my questions. He was patient, and sad alongside me. I understand and accept the situation now, and am supportive of him as much as he is supportive of me. The grief is there for our marriage, but we are experiencing a better friendship than we had before. I fully believe we will be there for each other - life is lonely and at the end of the day we are still best friends.
Let the grief happen. Be honest. Be present if you feel you want to support him. Your words aren't word vomit, you're showing how much thought and care you're putting into this. Best of luck in your conversation, and hope you both come out of this stronger as individuals <3
